source.title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
source.authors: Jing-Nan Zheng; Cheng Jin; Ming Zhang; Huan-Chen Sun; Zhong-Tian Ma; Kai-Sen Yang; Zi-Yuan Zhou; Tong Wu; Dong-Cheng Zhang; Yi Zhang; Xiao Wang; Han Qi; Shu Yu; Er-Mo Hua; Zong-Ji Yu; Chao-Zhuo Li; Xiaoyu Wen; Zhe-Kai Chen; Jia-Wei Zhou; Si-Rui Chen; Ning Ding; An Zhang; Tat-Seng Chua; Xiang-Nan He; Xia Hu; Bo-Wen Zhou; Qiao-Sheng Zhang; You-Bang Sun; Xiang Wang; Zhong Huang; Chao-Chao Lu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares RMU-style in-place removal and REX expert excision, including how their WMDP results change after post-training. It argues that shared-parameter unlearning suppresses expression and reports rebound after training, while structural excision is more persistent.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's WMDP results for RMU, REX, and subsequent training, plus MMLU capability measurements and the reported ReSI update. The paper also discusses earlier studies on recovery, which are cited findings and are not recorded as rows. POGB reasoning results do not bear on the claim. Table 4 reports the kept-share figures as removal-retention summaries; the individual WMDP accuracy rows are recorded instead.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3.1 and Table 4 apply an RMU recipe to Safin-1-35B-A3B and run 250M tokens of standard SFT. WMDP-Bio rebounds from 56.9% to 81.7%, which bears on A and B. The study also tests whether its REX expert excision resists the same post-training and a ReSI round (F). Its own WMDP/MMLU numbers bear on these versions. It does not test internal-edit, quantization or prompt-only recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that in-place RMU removal almost entirely disappears under 250M tokens of standard post-training. REX keeps about 90% of its removal on the public model, but only when training is done on the recombined full model and experts are excised at deployment. Removal also carries through a ReSI round with small MMLU cost. The authors are the developers of REX and Safin.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates REX, an architectural relocation-and-excision method, against an RMU cleanup recipe and subsequent training. It does not reproduce the original claim's full set of unlearning attacks or recovery interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on whether post-training is performed on the recombined full structure followed by excision (A3) or directly on the excised public model (A3-direct). WMDP rebound also differs by domain and between RMU and REX.

fits_no_version.finding: ReSI reduces jailbreak ASR (H-CoT 82→14%, X-Teaming 64.78→32.08%). These measure harmful-request compliance, not recovery of unlearned knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-alignment robustness to jailbreaks (not knowledge unlearning).

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the WMDP or MMLU results. The recovery comparison uses one 250M-token standard SFT setup and one ReSI round; it does not test few-example relearning, quantization, prompt-only attacks, or activation-direction ablation. WMDP accuracies for the REX public model are above the stated 25% chance level, so the study does not show near-chance accuracy for both domains.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 also reports WMDP and MMLU values for F3 (the recombined full model after post-training). These are not included because F3 retains the removable experts and is not the deployed, excised unlearned model. The table's kept-share summaries are described in notes rather than entered as separate rows because the underlying domain-specific accuracy rows are included.

untested.parts: Prompt-based, quantization and activation-ablation attacks on RMU; only one RMU recipe on one model.
Small relearning sets, loosely related data, and subsets of forgotten facts. Only 250M-token general SFT was tested.
Entirely untested: no direction ablation or internal analysis. The suppression-not-deletion statement is asserted, citing prior work.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context recovery of WMDP knowledge not tested.
REX is not tested against targeted relearning on forget-set data, quantization, ablation or prompt attacks; only general SFT and ReSI.

missing.what: MMLU for R (82.0%), R-SFT (82.4%) and A3-direct (80.7%). R's value shows RMU kept general ability, which A needs.
MMLU-Pro/IFEval for Safin-1 vs Safin-1.5 (77.10→76.80; 85.58→87.06) and for Safin-1+REX (79.20, 92.61). These show the capability cost of REX plus ReSI.

record.verdict_notes: Self-evaluation of the authors' own method (REX, ref [30]); single model, no uncertainty reported. The RMU comparison uses the light-cleanup RMU budget tuned for REX, not a full-strength RMU, so RMU's weak initial removal may reflect that choice. The post-ReSI WMDP values are compared against Safin-1 in the record; A3 (40.8/32.5) is the more informative baseline.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests WMDP accuracy and MMLU retention for its RMU and REX routes, including after post-training. It does not test activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery.
Tests 250M-token standard post-training and one ReSI update, not recovery from a few examples, unrelated or loosely related examples specifically, or a subset of forgotten facts.

The authors argue that in-place RMU suppresses expression rather than removing knowledge and report a post-training rebound. They do not ablate an activation direction or directly measure the proposed internal access mechanism.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreak prompts, other languages, and in-context information as recovery methods are not tested.
REX is evaluated against standard 250M-token post-training and a ReSI update. It is not tested against activation ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks.

relation.reason: Table 4 reports results on recovery after RMU and on REX resistance.

tranche.reason: The study reports results showing version A fails: RMU leaves Bio at 56.9% and SFT returns it to 81.7% (3.4% kept). Sec 2.2 argues that in-place removal suppresses rather than deletes. For A it uses the original's own method and measure (RMU, WMDP), so T2 is not a better fit.

source_check.notes: The authors include Cheng Jin, first author of REX (2610.25791), so this is a test by REX's own authors: one model, one SFT recipe and seed, no WMDP error bars. R is the light cleanup RMU (32M tokens, layers 7–9), not a standalone-tuned RMU. The delivered route is training by the developer; the attacker-like case is A3-direct. The 40.8/64.0 values are Safin-1+REX; released Safin-1.5 scores 43.68 on Bio. The authors' 'over 96%' MMLU retention is 95.9% from Table 4.

statements.correction: Cheng Jin, first author of REX (2610.25791, ref [30]), is a co-first author of 2610.40751. R-SFT: Bio 56.9 to 81.7 vs B 82.6 (r7).
statements.problem: Gives no number for this study. Its 250M-token SFT budget matches. The hedged 'may share a group' is confirmed by the text.

statements.correction: R-SFT: Bio 56.9 to 81.7 (3.4% of removal kept), Cyber 32.7 to 47.2 (43.6% kept).
statements.problem: Names no number from this study. Its cited rows fit the claim.
Makes no claim about this study.
The REX numbers come from 2610.25791. Nothing wrong is said about this study, and its rows r11-r17 fit the delivered-route claim.

statements.correction: A3-direct (excised A2 fine-tuned directly, 250M-token SFT): Bio 36.2 to 64.0 (40.0% kept), Cyber 29.5 to 41.8 (57.5% kept). Delivered route A3: Bio 40.8, Cyber 32.5.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: RMU route followed by 250M-token standard post-training
reader_labels.reason: The RMU route rises to 81.7% Bio and 47.2% Cyber after post-training, so simple continued training does not leave its initial suppression intact (r7–r8). The initial RMU values are also above the stated chance level (r3–r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: REX excision followed by 250M-token post-training or one ReSI round
reader_labels.reason: REX retains most of the removal under these updates, but WMDP values remain above chance and the paper does not test the full set of attacks in the claim (r11–r12, r16–r17).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RMU followed by 250M-token standard full-parameter SFT
reader_labels.reason: Bio accuracy rebounds nearly to the original-model value, and Cyber accuracy also rises after post-training (r7–r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: REX-excised public model followed by standard post-training or ReSI
reader_labels.reason: The reported REX routes show much smaller rebounds than RMU, and the ReSI-updated excised model remains substantially below Safin-1 on both WMDP domains (r11–r12, r16–r17). These experiments use large-scale standard post-training or a ReSI safety update, not a few-example relearning set.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RMU route followed by standard post-training
reader_labels.reason: The authors characterize in-place RMU as suppressing expression rather than removing knowledge, and the post-training WMDP rebound is consistent with that account (r7–r8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: REX with 250M-token standard post-training, and one ReSI update
reader_labels.reason: After training and excision, the REX public model retains most of its initial WMDP removal; the authors also report that removal carries through the ReSI round (r11–r12, r16–r17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Training directly on the excised public model raises WMDP accuracy to 64.0% Bio and 41.8% Cyber, showing that the result depends on training the recombined model and excising at deployment (r9–r10).
